finding: The uncited pretransplant VCUG paragraph reverses the native-ureter selection principle: reflux into the recipient ureter does not make that ureter a protective route for graft drainage.
evidence: Opened EAU Renal Transplantation guideline (2026), https://uroweb.org/guidelines/renal-transplantation/chapter/the-guideline, §3.1.5.d: primary pyelo- or ureteroureterostomy is described in recipients with non-refluxing native ureters; Lich-Gregoir is strongly recommended for normal anatomy. Opened Canadian transplant guideline https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1330435/: VCUG is selective when reflux or lower-tract abnormalities are suspected.

edit.old: Voiding cystourethrography is not routine before transplant, but may be obtained when the native ESRD cause raises suspicion for vesicoureteral reflux. Confirmed bilateral reflux into the native bladder favors ureteroureterostomy or pyeloureterostomy to the native ureter over a standard ureteroneocystostomy, since implanting the allograft ureter into a refluxing native bladder recreates the reflux the transplant would otherwise avoid. This selection criterion is upstream of, and distinct from, the salvage/difficult-bladder indication for UU above.
edit.new: Voiding cystourethrography is considered selectively when the cause of kidney failure or urinary history suggests vesicoureteral reflux or lower-tract dysfunction. Reflux into a native ureter does not favor using that ureter for allograft drainage: primary pyelo- or ureteroureterostomy has been described for a suitable non-refluxing native ureter, while clinically significant reflux and bladder dysfunction need separate pretransplant assessment.<sup>[[35]](#ref35)</sup>

finding: The ureteroureterostomy table combines a 1.5% fistula rate and a 4.7% obstruction rate into a false complication range, then presents a single retrospective comparison as a general fistula advantage.
evidence: Opened Nie et al. PubMed abstract PMID 19595183, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19595183/: among 275 UU recipients, 4 fistulas (1.5%) and 13 obstructions (4.7%); among 948 ureteroneocystostomy recipients, 39 fistulas (4.1%) and 22 obstructions (2.3%). These are different endpoints in a retrospective cohort.

edit.old: | **Ureteroureterostomy (UU)** | End-to-end or end-to-side anastomosis of donor ureter to native ureter | **1.5–4.7%** | Lower fistula rate (1.5% vs. 4.1%, p < 0.05); preserves a non-refluxing system; useful in difficult bladders or as salvage<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[15]](#ref15)</sup> |
edit.new: | **Ureteroureterostomy (UU)** | End-to-end or end-to-side anastomosis of donor ureter to a suitable native ureter | Fistula: 4/275 (1.5%); obstruction: 13/275 (4.7%) in one retrospective cohort | In Nie's cohort, UU was associated with fewer fistulas than ureteroneocystostomy (4/275 vs. 39/948) but more obstruction (13/275 vs. 22/948); recipient-ureter reflux status and anatomy matter.<sup>[[40]](#ref40)[[35]](#ref35)</sup> |

finding: The Key Points claim of graft loss below 5% in contemporary fistula series is unsupported by its citations, which mix eras and fistula with other ureteral complications.
evidence: Opened Nie PubMed abstract PMID 19545693 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19545693/: transplant nephrectomy in 1/43 fistula patients; opened Buresley PubMed abstract PMID 18790231 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18790231/: no graft loss among 15 leaks. Illésy 2022 indexed publisher/PubMed abstract reports graftectomy in 2/40 patients with mixed ureteral-anastomosis complications, not a fistula-specific rate.

edit.old: | **Graft loss from fistula** | Rare (< 5%) in contemporary series<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[3]](#ref3)[[16]](#ref16)</sup> |
edit.new: | **Graft loss from fistula** | One transplant nephrectomy among 43 fistula patients in Nie's 2009 series; Buresley's 2008 series reported no graft loss among 15 leaks. These series do not establish a universal contemporary rate.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[13]](#ref13)</sup> |

finding: The 10–15% graft-loss and up-to-15% mortality figures are background estimates for urological complications overall, not estimates for delayed diagnosis of urinary fistula.
evidence: Opened Li Marzi et al. PubMed abstract PMID 16182729, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16182729/: its introduction attributes 10–15% graft loss and up to 15% mortality to urological complications generally; the abstract does not define a delayed-diagnosis fistula subgroup.

edit.old: | Historical graft loss / mortality with delayed diagnosis | **10–15%** graft loss / up to **15%** mortality<sup>[[2]](#ref2)</sup> |
edit.new: | Historical urological complications (all types) | The 2005 report cited 10–15% graft loss and up to 15% mortality for urological complications overall; these are neither fistula-specific nor delayed-diagnosis estimates.<sup>[[2]](#ref2)</sup> |

finding: The 95% functioning-graft figure is discharge status after intervention for mixed ureteral-anastomotic complications, not a fistula closure or long-term graft-survival result.
evidence: Illésy et al. 2022 publisher-indexed abstract https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0041134522007151 and PubMed indexed abstract https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36400590/: 40/433 recipients had an intervention-requiring ureteral-anastomotic complication, 38/40 left hospital with a functioning graft; no fistula-only denominator or long-term endpoint is reported in the abstract. Direct publisher/PubMed opening was blocked, so this finding rests on the complete indexed abstract.

edit.old: | Discharged with functioning graft after treatment | **95%**<sup>[[16]](#ref16)</sup> |
edit.new: | Functioning graft at discharge after intervention for mixed ureteral-anastomotic complications | 38/40 (95%); the cohort was not limited to urinary fistula.<sup>[[16]](#ref16)</sup> |

finding: The antegrade-pyelography sensitivity range promotes an initial-detection proportion and repeat-study yield from a 12-patient series into general test sensitivity.
evidence: Opened Smith et al. PubMed abstract PMID 3044039, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3044039/: initial antegrade pyelography detected 10/12 proven leaks (83%); the remaining two appeared on follow-up nephrostograms within 24 hours. Opened Matalon PubMed abstract PMID 2305088 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2305088/ does not supply a comparative sensitivity estimate.

edit.old: Most accurate test, 83–100% sensitivity; directly demonstrates the leak site<sup>[[25]](#ref25)[[26]](#ref26)</sup>
edit.new: In a 12-patient series of proven leaks, initial antegrade pyelography demonstrated 10/12 (83%); repeat nephrostograms detected the remaining two within 24 hours and helped localize the leak.<sup>[[25]](#ref25)</sup>

finding: The 'other' etiologic risks mix early fistula, combined fistula/stenosis, and all-urological-complication endpoints without telling the reader which association applies to which event.
evidence: Opened Neri PubMed abstract PMID 19460524 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19460524/: male recipient sex HR 2.5 for early fistula, while HR 2.0 male sex and first transplant HR 0.4 concern combined fistula/stenosis. Opened Buresley PMID 18790231 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18790231/: cadaveric-donor association concerns all urologic complications.

edit.old: 7. **Other.** Male recipient sex (HR 2.0, p < 0.05), retransplantation (first transplant protective, HR 0.4, p < 0.05), and cadaveric donor.<sup>[[4]](#ref4)[[13]](#ref13)</sup>
edit.new: 7. **Other reported associations.** In Neri's retrospective cohort, male recipient sex was associated with early fistula (HR 2.5); male sex (HR 2.0) and repeat transplantation related to the combined fistula/stenosis endpoint. Buresley associated cadaveric donation with urological complications overall.<sup>[[4]](#ref4)[[13]](#ref13)</sup>

finding: The Key Points risk row repeats predictors from necrosis and combined complication studies as if all were validated fistula risk factors.
evidence: Opened Karam PubMed abstract PMID 15371676 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15371676/: donor age and DGF predict ureteral necrosis; opened Neri PMID 19460524: retransplantation belongs to a fistula/stenosis combined endpoint. Rahnemai-Azar's indexed PubMed abstract (ref10) associates renal-artery multiplicity with all early urologic complications.

edit.old: | **Key risk factors** | Donor age, DGF, renal-artery multiplicity, male recipient sex, retransplantation<sup>[[3]](#ref3)[[4]](#ref4)[[6]](#ref6)</sup> |
edit.new: | **Reported associations** | Ureteral necrosis: donor age and DGF; early urologic complications overall: renal-artery multiplicity; early fistula: male recipient sex in one retrospective series; combined fistula/stenosis: repeat transplantation.<sup>[[4]](#ref4)[[6]](#ref6)[[10]](#ref10)</sup> |

finding: The 6.15% and 8.33% table figures are overall urologic-complication rates in one retrospective 524-recipient comparison, not pooled rates or demonstrated leak-rate differences.
evidence: Opened Baston et al. abstract reprint https://www.urotoday.com/2014-09-18-02-47-34/renal-vascular-disease/68622-comparative-urologic-complications-of-ureteroneocystostomy-in-kidney-transplantation-transvesical-leadbetter-politano-versus-extravesical-lich-gregoir-technique-abstract.html (PMID 24507047): 6.15% vs 8.33% overall complications, p = 0.06, similar leak rates. Opened Alberts et al. full text https://pure.eur.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/99620379/Transplant_International_-_2014_-_Alberts.pdf: 26-study pooled leak RR 0.47 (0.30–0.75) is a separate estimate.

edit.old: | **Lich-Gregoir (extravesical)** | Mucosal nick, ureteral anastomosis from outside the bladder, submucosal tunnel by seromuscular reapproximation | **6.15%** overall | Lower complication rate, less technically demanding; slight residual leak / reflux risk<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[2]](#ref2)[[14]](#ref14)</sup> |
edit.new: | **Lich-Gregoir (extravesical)** | Mucosal nick, ureteral anastomosis from outside the bladder, submucosal tunnel by seromuscular reapproximation | 6.15% overall urologic complications in one 524-recipient cohort | The cohort comparison with Leadbetter-Politano was not statistically significant (p = 0.06); a separate meta-analysis found lower pooled leakage with Lich-Gregoir (RR 0.47).<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup> |

finding: The broad survival reassurance implies that prompt fistula treatment preserves long-term survival, although the long-term comparison concerns a single ureteral-necrosis cohort and the second citation gives only discharge outcomes.
evidence: Opened Karam PubMed abstract PMID 15371676 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15371676/: 52/1,629 developed ureteral necrosis; 10-year patient survival 87% vs 86% and graft survival 66% vs 58%, neither statistically significant. Illésy's indexed abstract reports discharge status for mixed complications, not long-term fistula outcomes.

edit.old: Despite the morbidity, long-term graft and patient survival are generally not compromised when the complication is recognized promptly and managed appropriately.<sup>[[6]](#ref6)[[16]](#ref16)</sup>
edit.new: In Karam's retrospective cohort, 10-year patient and graft survival did not differ significantly between recipients with ureteral necrosis (52/1,629) and controls.<sup>[[6]](#ref6)</sup>

finding: The unstented modified-technique result needs its 12-month endpoint and single-surgeon observational setting; it does not test omission of a stent against routine stenting.
evidence: Opened Ciancio et al. PLoS One full text https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0244248 (PMID 33428659): 500 consecutive recipients operated by one surgeon, 7/500 urologic complications and 5/500 leaks during the first 12 months, without a randomized stented comparator.

edit.old: A modified extravesical technique (mobilized bladder, longer ureteral spatulation, inclusion of bladder mucosa with detrusor in the anastomosis) achieved a urologic-complication rate of 1.4% (7/500) without routine stenting.<sup>[[17]](#ref17)</sup>
edit.new: In Ciancio's single-surgeon retrospective series of 500 recipients, a modified unstented extravesical technique was followed by 7/500 urologic complications (1.4%), including 5/500 leaks (1.0%), in the first 12 months.<sup>[[17]](#ref17)</sup>

finding: A 2026 follow-on report expands the page's cited 500-recipient unstented technique series to 697 recipients; it is relevant context but remains uncontrolled and does not overturn randomized stenting evidence. Add this as context after the corrected 2021 series sentence.
evidence: Opened Ciancio et al. PubMed abstract PMID 42446792, DOI 10.1007/s11255-026-05249-3, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42446792/: one surgeon's 697 consecutive adult kidney-alone recipients, 16/697 (2.3%) with any urologic complication and 14/697 (2.0%) with leak or obstruction/stricture (including suspected events) in the first 12 months; authors explicitly say equivalence to optimized stented Lich-Gregoir cannot be concluded without a direct control group.

finding: The EAU Lich-Gregoir recommendation is limited to recipients with normal urological anatomy and is paired with a strong native-ureter alternative when the transplant ureter is short or poorly vascularized.
evidence: Opened EAU 2026 renal transplantation guideline https://uroweb.org/guidelines/renal-transplantation/chapter/the-guideline, §3.1.5.d, recommendation table: Lich-Gregoir for normal urological anatomy, Strong; pyelo-/ureteroureteral anastomosis for very short or poorly vascularized transplant ureter, Strong.

edit.old: The EAU Renal Transplantation guideline gives a strong recommendation to use transplant ureteric stents prophylactically and a strong recommendation for a Lich-Gregoir-type extravesical anastomosis.<sup>[[35]](#ref35)</sup>
edit.new: The EAU Renal Transplantation guideline strongly recommends prophylactic transplant ureteric stenting and a Lich-Gregoir-type extravesical anastomosis for recipients with normal urological anatomy; it also strongly recommends pyelo- or ureteroureteral anastomosis as an alternative for a very short or poorly vascularized transplant ureter.<sup>[[35]](#ref35)</sup>

finding: The 7% to 2% series changed both anastomotic technique and stenting policy over time, so the wording attributes a nonrandomized before/after difference to their combination as though it were a causal effect.
evidence: Moreno-Alarcón et al. PubMed abstract PMID 24507045 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24507045/: first 700 recipients had mixed anastomoses and selective stenting; subsequent 311 had Lich-Gregoir with universal stents; fistula 7% vs 2% (p = 0.0001). This design cannot isolate stent, technique, or era effects.

edit.old: Combining Lich-Gregoir with routine double-J stenting reduced fistula rates from 7% to 2% (p = 0.0001) in a 1,011-transplant single-center series.<sup>[[21]](#ref21)</sup>
edit.new: In a nonrandomized single-center series, fistula occurred in 7% of the first 700 recipients treated with mixed anastomotic techniques and selective double-J stenting, versus 2% of the next 311 treated with Lich-Gregoir and universal double-J stenting (p = 0.0001); the effects of technique, stenting, and era cannot be separated.<sup>[[21]](#ref21)</sup>

finding: The 2026 pooled UTI result uses varying trial definitions, including culture positivity alone; an unqualified 'UTI' can be read as symptomatic infection.
evidence: Opened Yin et al. PeerJ full text https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12861130/ (PMID 41630842): UTI outcome from 14 trials, RR 1.41 (95% CI 1.08–1.84), I² = 54%; definitions varied and some studies counted a positive culture without symptoms.

edit.old: - Pooled RR for UTI with stenting: 1.41 (1.08–1.84)<sup>[[19]](#ref19)</sup>
edit.new: - Pooled RR for trial-defined UTI with stenting: 1.41 (1.08–1.84) across 14 trials; some definitions included a positive culture without symptoms.<sup>[[19]](#ref19)</sup>

finding: The cited ACR criteria address urinary obstruction and generic postoperative ureteral injury rather than a transplant-specific PCN recommendation; the EAU guideline supplies the direct transplant-leak recommendation.
evidence: Opened Scheidt et al. ACR criteria PubMed abstract PMID 32370972 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32370972/: Radiologic Management of Urinary Tract Obstruction is the document's scope. Opened EAU 2026 renal guideline https://uroweb.org/guidelines/renal-transplantation/chapter/the-guideline, §3.1.7.h: Strong recommendation for JJ stent and bladder catheter and/or PCN for urine leak. The ACR detailed ratings could not be opened; no transplant-specific claim is inferred from them.

edit.old: PCN is recommended in the ACR Appropriateness Criteria for transplant urinary obstruction / leak<sup>[[27]](#ref27)</sup>
edit.new: PCN is among the decompression options the EAU strongly recommends for transplant urine leak, alongside JJ stenting and bladder catheter drainage.<sup>[[35]](#ref35)</sup>

finding: The percutaneous series includes only eight leaks and a 50% long-term patency result; it cannot alone support a blanket first-line rule for all feasible leaks, including massive or ischemic defects.
evidence: Opened Eldem PubMed abstract PMID 32370698 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32370698/: 27 total patients, 8 leaks and 50% long-term patency in the leak subgroup. Opened EAU 2026 guideline §3.1.7.h https://uroweb.org/guidelines/renal-transplantation/chapter/the-guideline: early low-volume leaks may receive diversion; massive leaks or failed conservative management require surgical repair.

edit.old: percutaneous management remains the first-line choice when feasible, with surgery for failure<sup>[[39]](#ref39)</sup>
edit.new: the authors favored initial percutaneous management in selected cases, while the EAU guideline calls for repair of massive leaks or failure of conservative management<sup>[[39]](#ref39)[[35]](#ref35)</sup>

finding: CMV/BK histology and long-term transplant-survival literature do not show that viral surveillance prevents late ureteral complications; the prevention effect is an unsupported causal inference.
evidence: Opened Karam PubMed abstract PMID 15371676 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15371676/: CMV inclusions 4/25 and BK inclusions 2/25 necrotic ureters examined, observational. Opened Hariharan et al. full-text review https://www.kidneyforlife.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/nejmra2014530.pdf: transplant viral surveillance is discussed for graft health, without a measured ureteral-complication reduction.

edit.old: 8. **CMV and BK virus surveillance.** Early detection and treatment may reduce late ureteral complications.<sup>[[6]](#ref6)[[34]](#ref34)</sup>
edit.new: 8. **CMV and BK virus surveillance.** Follow transplant-team monitoring protocols; CMV and BK inclusions were found in 4/25 and 2/25 necrotic ureters examined in one observational series. A reduction in late ureteral complications has not been established.<sup>[[6]](#ref6)[[34]](#ref34)</sup>

finding: The immunosuppression paragraph turns mTOR-regimen wound outcomes into an unmeasured ureteral-healing and steroid effect, while omitting the transplant-specific trial denominators.
evidence: Opened Pengel et al. systematic review full text https://www.frontierspartnerships.org/articles/10.1111/j.1432-2277.2011.01357.x/pdf (PMID 21955006): 37 solid-organ RCTs overall; kidney mTOR+CNI subgroup wound complications 12 trials, n = 4,787, OR 1.77 (1.31–2.37), lymphoceles 11 trials, n = 5,370, OR 2.07 (1.62–2.65); insufficient evidence to isolate a steroid effect or transplant-ureter anastomotic healing.

edit.old: Steroids and mTOR inhibitors impair tissue healing. In a systematic review of 37 RCTs, kidney recipients on mTOR inhibitors had more wound complications (OR 1.77 with calcineurin inhibitors) and lymphoceles (OR 2.07); a perigraft collection in these patients is therefore not always a urinoma, so confirm with fluid creatinine.<sup>[[38]](#ref38)</sup>
edit.new: In a systematic review of 37 solid-organ transplant RCTs, kidney recipients given an mTOR inhibitor plus a calcineurin inhibitor from transplantation had more wound complications (12 trials, n = 4,787; OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.31–2.37) and lymphoceles (11 trials, n = 5,370; OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.62–2.65) than recipients on regimens without an mTOR inhibitor. The review could not determine an independent steroid effect or ureteral-healing outcome. Confirm a suspected urinoma with fluid creatinine in context.<sup>[[38]](#ref38)</sup>

finding: No transplant-recipient series cited on this page establishes that a forgotten stent more often presents with graft dysfunction than urinary symptoms; the comparative claim could delay recognition of symptomatic retained stents.
evidence: Opened Bhuva et al. PMC full text PMID 19133113, DOI 10.1186/1757-1626-2-27, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2639559/: a 10-year retained transplant stent presented with irritative symptoms and satisfactory graft biochemistry. Opened Gosein et al. PubMed abstract PMID 39315954, DOI 10.1308/rcsann.2024.0066, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39315954/: a 19-year stent was found after hematuria without encrustation. Case reports do not establish a 'more often' comparison.

edit.old: Unlike the encrustation, stone formation and hematuria typical of a forgotten stent in the general population, a retained transplant stent more often presents as progressive graft dysfunction rather than obstructive symptoms, though recurrent UTI and encrustation can also occur.
edit.new: Retained transplant stents have been described with urinary symptoms, hematuria, recurrent UTI, encrustation, obstruction, and graft dysfunction; published case reports do not establish which presentation is most common.<sup>[[41]](#ref41)[[42]](#ref42)</sup>

finding: The retained-stent management sentence makes nephrostomy usual even though uncomplicated, unencrusted stents can be removed cystoscopically; intervention depends on encrustation and access.
evidence: Opened Gosein et al. PubMed abstract PMID 39315954 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39315954/: an unencrusted 19-year transplant stent was removed by flexible cystoscopy under local anesthesia. Opened Bhuva et al. full text https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2639559/: heavy encrustation required cystoscopic clearance plus percutaneous nephrolithotomy; nephrostomy may provide drainage/access but is not universal.

edit.old: Management usually requires urinary diversion with a nephrostomy tube and a retrograde, antegrade or combined endoscopic approach to remove the stent.
edit.new: Removal depends on encrustation and access: an unencrusted stent may be removed by flexible cystoscopy, while heavily encrusted stents may require retrograde, antegrade, or combined endoscopic procedures, with nephrostomy when drainage or access is needed.<sup>[[41]](#ref41)[[42]](#ref42)</sup>

finding: The Foley-removal Cochrane review cited for scrotal or labial edema contains no presentation data for urine leaks.
evidence: Opened Goodfellow et al. PubMed abstract PMID 37449968 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37449968/: the review compares early versus late urinary-catheter removal in two trials (197 recipients) and reports bacteriuria/UTI evidence, not edema presentation. The other cited references require separate support for the symptom.

evidence: STYLE.md §3, read from /Users/joyboy/Documents/WARWIKI/warwiki/STYLE.md: claim-bearing sentences need a subject and finite verb. Opened EAU 2026 renal guideline §3.1.7.h bases leak treatment on site, timing, volume and feasibility of diversion.

edit.new: Management depends on leak size and location, infection, and ureteral viability.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[2]](#ref2)[[9]](#ref9)[[22]](#ref22)</sup>
